title: Ὁπλομαχία, σόλος, πέλεια
titleEn: The Armed Duel, the Weight and the Dove — Iliad 23.797–897
part: The Armed Duel, the Weight and the Dove (23.797–897)
about: Achilles puts the armour of Sarpedon up as the prize for an armed duel, with the Thracian sword of Asteropaeus for the first to wound. Telamonian Ajax and Diomedes charge three times; Diomedes’ spear point reaches over Ajax’s shield toward his neck, and the Achaeans, afraid for Ajax, stop the fight and give equal prizes, and Achilles gives Diomedes the sword. Next he sets out a self-cast lump that once belonged to Eetion; the winner will have iron for five years. Polypoetes throws it beyond every other man, as far as a herdsman’s crook. For the archers Achilles ties a timorous dove to a ship’s mast. Teucer cuts the cord but has vowed nothing to Apollo; Meriones takes the bow, vows a hecatomb, and brings the dove down. Last Achilles lays out a spear and a cauldron for the javelin-throw, but sets Agamemnon above the contest and gives him the prize, and Agamemnon passes the spear to Meriones.

sentences.t: ὣς εἰπὼν ἐν χερσὶ τίθει, ὃ δ’ ἐδέξατο χαίρων.
sentences.l: So speaking, into his hands he put it, and he received it, rejoicing.
sentences.i: With these words he put it into his hands, and he took it gladly.
sentences.n: τίθει is an unaugmented imperfect of τίθημι (Attic ἐτίθει), ‘he put’. What Achilles puts into Antilochus’ hands is the half-talent of gold he promised in the last lines of the previous part. ὃ δ’ is the article as a pronoun, ‘and he’, Antilochus, and ἐδέξατο ‘received’ is the aorist of δέχομαι. The same line stands at 624, where another gift changes hands.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ Πηλεΐδης κατὰ μὲν δολιχόσκιον ἔγχος
θῆκ’ ἐς ἀγῶνα φέρων, κατὰ δ’ ἀσπίδα καὶ τρυφάλειαν
τεύχεα Σαρπήδοντος, ἅ μιν Πάτροκλος ἀπηύρα.
sentences.l:
But Peleus’-son, the long-shadowed spear
set down, bringing it into the gathering, and the shield and the helm,
the armour of Sarpedon, which Patroclus took away from him.
sentences.i: Then the son of Peleus brought the long-shadowed spear, the shield and the helmet, the armour of Sarpedon that Patroclus took from him, and set them down in the gathering.
sentences.n: Πηλεΐδης ‘son of Peleus’ is Achilles, now bringing out prizes for the next contest, an armed duel. κατὰ … θῆκε is split by tmesis: κατά ‘down’ comes before ἔγχος and again before ἀσπίδα, while θῆκ’ and φέρων ‘bringing’ come later. ἀγών is ‘gathering’, the place where the Achaeans sit to watch. τεύχεα Σαρπήδοντος ‘the armour of Sarpedon’ stands in apposition to what has just been set down, and the Greek does not say whether the spear is counted in it; ἅ is its relative, and ἀπηύρα ‘took away’ is a past tense of ἀπαυράω.

sentences.t: στῆ δ’ ὀρθὸς καὶ μῦθον ἐν Ἀργείοισιν ἔειπεν·
sentences.l: and he stood upright and spoke a word among the Argives:
sentences.i: He stood up straight and spoke a word among the Argives:
sentences.n: στῆ is the aorist of ἵστημι, ‘stood’, and ὀρθός ‘upright’ agrees with the subject, Achilles. μῦθον … ἔειπεν ‘spoke a word’ is a formula, and ἐν Ἀργείοισιν ‘among the Argives’ uses one of the poem’s names for the whole army. The colon introduces his offer of the armed duel, which runs to the end of line 810.

sentences.t:
ἄνδρε δύω περὶ τῶνδε κελεύομεν, ὥ περ ἀρίστω,
τεύχεα ἑσσαμένω ταμεσίχροα χαλκὸν ἑλόντε
ἀλλήλων προπάροιθεν ὁμίλου πειρηθῆναι.
sentences.l:
“Two men, for these things, we bid, who are the best,
having put on their armour, taking the skin-cutting bronze,
before the throng to make trial of each other.
sentences.i: “We call on two men, the best of you, for these prizes: to put on their armour, take up the skin-cutting bronze, and make trial of each other in front of the throng.
sentences.n: These are the terms of the duel. ἄνδρε δύω ‘two men’ is a dual, the Greek number for a pair, and so are the words that agree with it: ὥ (the relative ‘who’), ἀρίστω ‘the best’, ἑσσαμένω ‘having put on’ and ἑλόντε ‘having taken’. κελεύομεν ‘we bid’ has the two men as its object and πειρηθῆναι ‘to make trial’ (an aorist passive form with an active sense) as its infinitive; ἀλλήλων is ‘of one another’. ταμεσίχροα ‘skin-cutting’ describes the bronze, the weapon.

sentences.t:
ὁππότερός κε φθῇσιν ὀρεξάμενος χρόα καλόν,
ψαύσῃ δ’ ἐνδίνων διά τ’ ἔντεα καὶ μέλαν αἷμα,
sentences.l:
Whichever of the two shall be first, reaching out to the fair skin,
and shall touch the inward parts through the gear and the black blood,
sentences.i: Whichever of the two is first to thrust at the fair skin and reach the inward parts through the gear and the black blood,
sentences.n: φθῇσιν ‘shall be first’ is the aorist subjunctive of φθάνω, and κε gives the sense ‘whichever … shall’. ὀρεξάμενος ‘reaching out’ says how: the object is the fair skin, and the weapon, the spear, is understood. ψαύσῃ ‘shall touch’ takes the genitive ἐνδίνων ‘the inward parts’, a rare word. διά with the accusative means ‘through’ the gear (ἔντεα) and the black blood. The main clause comes in the next unit.

sentences.t:
τῷ μὲν ἐγὼ δώσω τόδε φάσγανον ἀργυρόηλον
καλὸν Θρηΐκιον, τὸ μὲν Ἀστεροπαῖον ἀπηύρων·
sentences.l:
to him I shall give this silver-studded sword,
fine, Thracian, which from Asteropaeus I took away;
sentences.i: I shall give him this silver-studded sword, a fine Thracian one, which I took from Asteropaeus;
sentences.n: τῷ μέν ‘to him’ answers ὁππότερος in the last unit. φάσγανον ἀργυρόηλον ‘silver-studded sword’ is the sword Achilles took from Asteropaeus, the Paeonian he killed at the river in book 21; Θρηΐκιον ‘Thracian’ is an adjective and gives the sword’s make. τὸ μέν is the relative ‘which’ in its old demonstrative form, and ἀπηύρων is a past tense of ἀπαυράω ‘take away’, the verb of 800.

sentences.t: τεύχεα δ’ ἀμφότεροι ξυνήϊα ταῦτα φερέσθων·
sentences.l: and the armour, these, both of them, as common goods let them carry off;
sentences.i: and let both of them carry off this armour as common goods;
sentences.n: φερέσθων is a third-person imperative of φέρω in the middle voice, ‘let them carry off’, each for himself. ξυνήϊα ‘common goods’ has the old spelling ξυν- and goes with τεύχεα … ταῦτα ‘these arms’: the armour of Sarpedon set out at 798–800 is to be shared by the two men, whoever wins the sword. ἀμφότεροι ‘both’ is the subject.

sentences.t: καί σφιν δαῖτ’ ἀγαθὴν παραθήσομεν ἐν κλισίῃσιν.
sentences.l: and for them a good feast we shall set before them in the huts.”
sentences.i: and we shall set a good feast before them in the huts.”
sentences.n: σφιν is the epic dative ‘for them’, the two fighters. παραθήσομεν ‘we shall set beside, set before’ is the future of παρατίθημι, and ἀγαθήν is ‘good’. κλισίῃσιν is the epic dative plural of κλισίη ‘hut’, the Achaeans’ huts by the ships. The closing quotation mark ends Achilles’ offer, which began at 802.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἔφατ’, ὦρτο δ’ ἔπειτα μέγας Τελαμώνιος Αἴας,
ἂν δ’ ἄρα Τυδεΐδης ὦρτο, κρατερὸς Διομήδης.
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and rose then great Telamonian Ajax,
and up rose Tydeus’-son, strong Diomedes.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and great Telamonian Ajax rose, and up rose the son of Tydeus, strong Diomedes.
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφατ’ ‘So he spoke’ is the formula that closes a speech. ὦρτο, the aorist middle of ὄρνυμι, means ‘rose’, and ἂν … ὦρτο is tmesis: ἀνά ‘up’ is separated from its verb. Τελαμώνιος ‘Telamonian’ tells this Ajax from the other, and Τυδεΐδης ‘son of Tydeus’ is Diomedes. The two who answer Achilles’ call for a pair are Ajax and Diomedes.

sentences.t:
οἳ δ’ ἐπεὶ οὖν ἑκάτερθεν ὁμίλου θωρήχθησαν,
ἐς μέσον ἀμφοτέρω συνίτην μεμαῶτε μάχεσθαι
δεινὸν δερκομένω·
sentences.i: And when the two had armed themselves on either side of the throng, they came together in the middle, both of them eager to fight, with dread looks;
sentences.n: θωρήχθησαν is the aorist passive of θωρήσσω, ‘had armed themselves’, with ἑκάτερθεν ὁμίλου ‘on either side of the throng’: each puts on his armour at his own end of the crowd. συνίτην is the dual imperfect of σύνειμι (from εἶμι), ‘came together’, and ἀμφοτέρω, μεμαῶτε and δερκομένω are duals agreeing with the pair. δεινὸν δερκομένω ‘looking dreadfully’ uses the neuter adjective as an adverb. The unit stops in the middle of line 815.

sentences.t: θάμβος δ’ ἔχε πάντας Ἀχαιούς.
sentences.l: and wonder held all the Achaeans.
sentences.i: and all the Achaeans were held in wonder.
sentences.n: θάμβος ‘wonder’ is the noun, and ἔχε ‘held’ is an unaugmented imperfect of ἔχω (Attic εἶχε). The object is πάντας Ἀχαιούς ‘all the Achaeans’, the onlookers. The unit begins in the middle of line 815, after the sign · that ends the previous unit.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅτε δὴ σχεδὸν ἦσαν ἐπ’ ἀλλήλοισιν ἰόντες,
τρὶς μὲν ἐπήϊξαν, τρὶς δὲ σχεδὸν ὁρμήθησαν.
sentences.l:
But when now they were near, advancing on one another,
three times they darted on, and three times they rushed close.
sentences.i: But when they were close and advancing on one another, three times they darted at each other, and three times they rushed close.
sentences.n: σχεδὸν ἦσαν ἰόντες ‘were near, advancing’ pairs ἦσαν with the participle ἰόντες ‘going’. ἐπήϊξαν is the aorist of ἐπαΐσσω ‘dart at’, and ὁρμήθησαν the aorist passive of ὁρμάω ‘rush’, with an active sense. τρὶς μέν … τρὶς δέ ‘three times … three times’ gives three charges before any blow is told; the blows follow in the next lines.

sentences.t:
ἔνθ’ Αἴας μὲν ἔπειτα κατ’ ἀσπίδα πάντοσ’ ἐΐσην
νύξ’, οὐδὲ χρό’ ἵκανεν·
sentences.l:
Then Ajax thereupon, at the shield equal on every side,
stabbed, but did not reach the skin;
sentences.i: Then Ajax stabbed at the shield, equal on every side, but did not reach the skin;
sentences.n: Ajax is the attacker here, and the shield (ἀσπίδα) is Diomedes’. νύξ’ is νύξε elided, an aorist of νύσσω ‘stab’ without the augment. πάντοσ’ ἐΐσην ‘equal on every side’ is the epithet of a round shield, even all round. χρό’ is χρόα elided, accusative of χρώς ‘skin’, and ἵκανεν is the imperfect of ἱκάνω ‘reach’, so the point never gets through to the body.

sentences.t: ἔρυτο γὰρ ἔνδοθι θώρηξ·
sentences.l: for within him guarded the breastplate;
sentences.i: for the breastplate guarded him within;
sentences.n: ἔρυτο ‘guarded’ is a past tense of ἐρύομαι ‘guard, protect’. The subject is θώρηξ ‘breastplate’, Diomedes’ own, and ἔνδοθι ‘within’ puts it behind the shield. γάρ gives the reason why the stab did not reach the skin.

sentences.t:
Τυδεΐδης δ’ ἄρ’ ἔπειτα ὑπὲρ σάκεος μεγάλοιο
αἰὲν ἐπ’ αὐχένι κῦρε φαεινοῦ δουρὸς ἀκωκῇ.
sentences.l:
And Tydeus’-son then, over the great shield,
ever at the neck kept on reaching with the tip of his shining spear.
sentences.i: And the son of Tydeus, over the great shield, kept reaching for Ajax’s neck with the tip of his shining spear.
sentences.n: ὑπὲρ σάκεος μεγάλοιο ‘over the great shield’ shows the angle: Diomedes thrusts over the top of Ajax’s shield, aiming at the neck. κῦρε is an imperfect of κύρω ‘light upon, reach’, with the dative αὐχένι ‘neck’, and αἰέν ‘ever’ makes it ‘kept on’; the Greek does not say that the point drew blood. ἀκωκῇ ‘tip’ is a dative of means, and φαεινοῦ ‘shining’ describes the spear.

sentences.t:
καὶ τότε δή ῥ’ Αἴαντι περιδείσαντες Ἀχαιοὶ
παυσαμένους ἐκέλευσαν ἀέθλια ἶσ’ ἀνελέσθαι.
sentences.l:
And then indeed, fearing greatly for Ajax, the Achaeans
gave orders, that having stopped they take up equal contest-prizes.
sentences.i: And then the Achaeans, in great fear for Ajax, gave orders that they stop and take equal prizes.
sentences.n: περιδείσαντες is the aorist participle of περιδείδω ‘fear greatly for’, with the dative Αἴαντι; the Achaeans fear for Ajax because Diomedes’ point is at his neck. ἐκέλευσαν ‘gave orders’ takes the accusative παυσαμένους ‘having stopped’ and the infinitive ἀνελέσθαι ‘to take up’. ἀέθλια ἶσα ‘equal contest-prizes’ means that no winner is named.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ Τυδεΐδῃ δῶκεν μέγα φάσγανον ἥρως
σὺν κολεῷ τε φέρων καὶ ἐϋτμήτῳ τελαμῶνι.
sentences.l:
But to Tydeus’-son gave the great sword the hero,
bringing it with its sheath and well-cut strap.
sentences.i: But the hero gave the son of Tydeus the great sword, bringing it with its sheath and its well-cut strap.
sentences.n: The subject of δῶκεν is ἥρως ‘the hero’, Achilles, and Τυδεΐδῃ is Diomedes in the dative. The μέγα φάσγανον ‘great sword’ is the Thracian one he offered at 807–808. φέρων ‘bringing’ goes with σὺν κολεῷ … τελαμῶνι ‘with sheath and strap’; the τελαμών is the strap that carries the sword, and ἐϋτμήτῳ means ‘well-cut’.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ Πηλεΐδης θῆκεν σόλον αὐτοχόωνον
ὃν πρὶν μὲν ῥίπτασκε μέγα σθένος Ἠετίωνος·
sentences.l:
But Peleus’-son set a self-cast lump,
which formerly used to throw the great strength of Eetion;
sentences.i: Then the son of Peleus set out a self-cast lump, which the great strength of Eetion used to throw in former days;
sentences.n: A new contest begins. σόλος is a lump of metal thrown for distance; its shape is not given, and it is often pictured as a discus. αὐτοχόωνος ‘self-cast’ is formed from αὐτο- ‘self’ and a root for ‘pour, cast’; it probably means cast as it stands, not forged. ῥίπτασκε is iterative, ‘used to throw’. μέγα σθένος Ἠετίωνος ‘the great strength of Eetion’ is a periphrasis for the man, as with Idomeneus at 13.248; Eetion is Andromache’s father, whom Achilles killed (6.414–416).

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἤτοι τὸν ἔπεφνε ποδάρκης δῖος Ἀχιλλεύς,
τὸν δ’ ἄγετ’ ἐν νήεσσι σὺν ἄλλοισι κτεάτεσσι.
sentences.l:
but indeed him killed swift-footed, heavenly Achilles,
and it he carried off in his ships with the other possessions.
sentences.i: but swift-footed, heavenly Achilles killed him, and carried it off in his ships with the other possessions.
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ἤτοι ‘but indeed’ turns from the old thrower to his fate. τὸν … ἔπεφνε is ‘killed him’ (aorist), and τὸν δ’ ἄγετ’ ‘and it he carried off’: ἄγετ’ is ἄγετο, the middle without the augment, ‘took for himself’, with the lump (masculine) as its object. κτεάτεσσι is the epic dative plural of κτέαρ ‘possession’, and σὺν ἄλλοισι ‘with the other’ puts the lump among the plunder.

sentences.t: στῆ δ’ ὀρθὸς καὶ μῦθον ἐν Ἀργείοισιν ἔειπεν·
sentences.l: and he stood upright and spoke a word among the Argives:
sentences.i: He stood up straight and spoke a word among the Argives:
sentences.n: στῆ is the aorist of ἵστημι, ‘stood’, and ὀρθός ‘upright’ agrees with the subject, Achilles. μῦθον … ἔειπεν ‘spoke a word’ is a formula, and ἐν Ἀργείοισιν ‘among the Argives’ is one of the poem’s names for the whole army. The colon introduces his call for throwers, which runs to line 835.

sentences.t:
ὄρνυσθ’ οἳ καὶ τούτου ἀέθλου πειρήσεσθε.
εἴ οἱ καὶ μάλα πολλὸν ἀπόπροθι πίονες ἀγροί,
sentences.l:
“Rise, you who of this contest also will make trial.
Even if for him very far off are his rich fields,
sentences.i: “Rise, you who will try your strength in this contest also. Even if his rich fields lie very far away,
sentences.n: ὄρνυσθ’ is the middle imperative of ὄρνυμι, ‘rise’; the sentence is the one Achilles used to call the runners at 753. οἳ … πειρήσεσθε is a relative clause with the future of πειράομαι ‘make trial’. The second sentence begins εἰ … καὶ μάλα ‘even if very’, and οἱ ‘for him’ is the owner of the fields, the winner; the verb ‘are’ is understood. The main clause comes in the next unit.

sentences.t:
ἕξει μιν καὶ πέντε περιπλομένους ἐνιαυτοὺς
χρεώμενος·
sentences.l:
he will have it, even for five years as they roll round,
using it;
sentences.i: he will have it to use even for five years as they roll round;
sentences.n: ἕξει μιν ‘he will have it’ is the main clause: the winner will keep the lump for πέντε περιπλομένους ἐνιαυτούς ‘five years as they roll round’, an accusative of duration. χρεώμενος is the Ionic form of χράομαι ‘use’, so ‘using it’. The next unit gives the reason, that he will not need to send to town for iron. The unit ends in the middle of line 834.

sentences.t:
οὐ μὲν γάρ οἱ ἀτεμβόμενός γε σιδήρου
ποιμὴν οὐδ’ ἀροτὴρ εἶσ’ ἐς πόλιν, ἀλλὰ παρέξει.
sentences.l:
for not indeed will, for him, cheated of iron,
shepherd or ploughman go to the city, but it will supply it.”
sentences.i: for no shepherd or ploughman of his, cheated of iron, will go into the city; the lump will supply it.”
sentences.n: οὐ μὲν γάρ … ‘for … not’ gives the reason. ἀτεμβόμενος σιδήρου ‘cheated of iron’ uses ἀτέμβομαι with the genitive and means left without it; the shepherd and ploughman belong to the winner (οἱ ‘his’). εἶσ’ is εἶσι, ‘will go’, and the subject of παρέξει ‘will supply’ is the lump, which is evidently iron. The closing quotation mark ends Achilles’ call, which began at 831.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἔφατ’, ὦρτο δ’ ἔπειτα μενεπτόλεμος Πολυποίτης,
ἂν δὲ Λεοντῆος κρατερὸν μένος ἀντιθέοιο,
ἂν δ’ Αἴας Τελαμωνιάδης καὶ δῖος Ἐπειός.
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and rose then Polypoetes, steadfast in battle,
and up the strong might of godlike Leonteus,
and up Ajax, Telamon’s-son, and heavenly Epeius.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and Polypoetes, steadfast in battle, rose, and up rose the strong might of godlike Leonteus, and up rose Ajax, son of Telamon, and heavenly Epeius.
sentences.n: The tmesis of 811–812 returns: ἂν δὲ … ἂν δ’ … ‘and up … and up …’ carries ὦρτο from the first clause. Λεοντῆος κρατερὸν μένος ἀντιθέοιο ‘the strong might of godlike Leonteus’ is a periphrasis for the man himself. Αἴας Τελαμωνιάδης is ‘Ajax, Telamon’s son’, and δῖος Ἐπειός ‘heavenly Epeius’ is the man who won the boxing earlier in this book. μενεπτόλεμος ‘steadfast in battle’ is Polypoetes’ stock epithet.

sentences.t: ἑξείης δ’ ἵσταντο, σόλον δ’ ἕλε δῖος Ἐπειός,
sentences.l: and in order they stood, and the lump took heavenly Epeius,
sentences.i: They took their stand in order, and heavenly Epeius took the lump,
sentences.n: ἑξείης ‘in order’ says that they take position in a row, and ἵσταντο is the imperfect middle of ἵστημι, ‘were taking their stand’. ἕλε ‘took’ is the aorist of αἱρέω without the augment (Attic εἷλε). σόλον is the lump of 826, and Epeius throws first, in the next unit.

sentences.t: ἧκε δὲ δινήσας·
sentences.l: and he threw it, having whirled it;
sentences.i: he whirled it round and let it fly;
sentences.n: ἧκε is the aorist of ἵημι ‘let go’, and δινήσας ‘having whirled’ the aorist participle of δινέω, the swing before the release. The subject, Epeius, carries over from the line before. The unit is short because the line holds two sentences; the sign · ends the first.

sentences.t: γέλασαν δ’ ἐπὶ πάντες Ἀχαιοί.
sentences.l: and laughed at him all the Achaeans.
sentences.i: and all the Achaeans laughed at him.
sentences.n: ἐπὶ … γέλασαν is tmesis for ἐπεγέλασαν ‘laughed at’; the Greek does not say why, but the laughter, set against Polypoetes’ throw at 844–847, implies that Epeius threw poorly. πάντες Ἀχαιοί ‘all the Achaeans’ are the onlookers.

sentences.t: δεύτερος αὖτ’ ἀφέηκε Λεοντεὺς ὄζος Ἄρηος·
sentences.l: second in turn let go Leonteus, scion of Ares;
sentences.i: Leonteus, scion of Ares, was second to let it go;
sentences.n: δεύτερος ‘second’ agrees with Λεοντεύς, and αὖτ’ is αὖτε ‘in turn’. ἀφέηκε is the epic form of ἀφῆκε, aorist of ἀφίημι ‘let go’ (the verb of ἧκε at 840). ὄζος Ἄρηος ‘scion of Ares’ is a stock title; ὄζος is literally ‘branch’. It was also given to Leonteus at 2.745.

sentences.t:
τὸ τρίτον αὖτ’ ἔρριψε μέγας Τελαμώνιος Αἴας
χειρὸς ἄπο στιβαρῆς, καὶ ὑπέρβαλε σήματα πάντων.
sentences.l:
the third in turn threw great Telamonian Ajax
from a stout hand, and passed beyond the marks of all.
sentences.i: Third, great Telamonian Ajax threw in his turn, from his stout hand, and passed beyond the marks of all.
sentences.n: τὸ τρίτον is a neuter adjective used as an adverb, ‘third’, and ἔρριψε is the aorist of ῥίπτω ‘throw’. χειρὸς ἄπο is ἀπὸ χειρός with the preposition placed after its noun. σήματα ‘marks’ are the places where the earlier throws landed, and ὑπέρβαλε ‘passed beyond’ takes the genitive πάντων ‘of all’; Ajax out-throws everyone so far.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅτε δὴ σόλον εἷλε μενεπτόλεμος Πολυποίτης,
ὅσσόν τίς τ’ ἔρριψε καλαύροπα βουκόλος ἀνήρ,
ἣ δέ θ’ ἑλισσομένη πέτεται διὰ βοῦς ἀγελαίας,
sentences.l:
But when now the lump took Polypoetes, steadfast in battle,
as far as some cowherd man throws a crook,
which, turning, flies through the cattle of the herd,
sentences.i: But when Polypoetes, steadfast in battle, took up the lump, as far as a cowherd throws a crook, which flies, turning round, through the cattle of the herd,
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ὅτε δὴ … opens a comparison that ends in the next unit with τόσσον ‘so far’. ὅσσον … ἔρριψε is a general (gnomic) aorist, ‘as far as a cowherd throws’. καλαύροψ is a herdsman’s staff, here thrown; the Greek says only that it is thrown and flies through the herd. ἑλισσομένη ‘turning round’ is a participle describing its flight, and βοῦς ἀγελαίας ‘cattle of the herd’ is the herd it passes through.

sentences.t: τόσσον παντὸς ἀγῶνος ὑπέρβαλε·
sentences.l: so far he passed beyond the whole gathering;
sentences.i: so far did he pass beyond the whole gathering;
sentences.n: τόσσον ‘so far’ answers ὅσσον in 845, and ὑπέρβαλε ‘passed beyond’ is the verb of 843 again, now with παντὸς ἀγῶνος. ἀγών is ‘gathering’ in the house rendering; whether the poet means the whole field or every competitor in it is not clear, and the English keeps the Greek’s words.

sentences.t: τοὶ δὲ βόησαν.
sentences.l: and they shouted.
sentences.i: and they shouted.
sentences.n: τοί is the old form of the article, equal to οἱ, ‘they’, here the onlookers who laughed at Epeius’ throw (840). βόησαν is the aorist of βοάω ‘shout’.

sentences.t:
ἀνστάντες δ’ ἕταροι Πολυποίταο κρατεροῖο
νῆας ἔπι γλαφυρὰς ἔφερον βασιλῆος ἄεθλον.
sentences.l:
And rising up, the companions of strong Polypoetes
bore to the hollow ships the king’s prize.
sentences.i: And the companions of strong Polypoetes stood up and carried the king’s prize to the hollow ships.
sentences.n: ἀνστάντες is ἀναστάντες, the aorist participle ‘having stood up’. βασιλῆος ἄεθλον ‘the king’s prize’ is Polypoetes’ prize, the lump itself (826–829), and βασιλεύς is a title of respect for a leader. ἔπι is ἐπί placed after its noun νῆας, ‘to the ships’, and γλαφυράς ‘hollow’ is the stock epithet.

sentences.t: αὐτὰρ ὃ τοξευτῇσι τίθει ἰόεντα σίδηρον,
sentences.l: But he for the archers set out dark iron,
sentences.i: Then for the archers he set out dark iron,
sentences.n: A new contest begins, the archery. τοξευτῇσι is the epic dative plural of τοξευτής ‘archer’, and τίθει an unaugmented imperfect, ‘set out’. ἰόεντα is ‘violet-coloured, dark’, from ἴον ‘violet’; whether it means dark-hued or rusty is not known, since ἰός can also mean ‘rust’. σίδηρος is ‘iron’, here the iron axe-heads of the next line.

sentences.t: κὰδ δ’ ἐτίθει δέκα μὲν πελέκεας, δέκα δ’ ἡμιπέλεκκα,
sentences.l: and down he laid ten axes, and ten half-axes,
sentences.i: and he laid down ten axes and ten half-axes,
sentences.n: κὰδ is κατά with its last letter assimilated to the δ that follows, and κὰδ … ἐτίθει is tmesis, ‘laid down’. πέλεκυς ‘axe’ and ἡμιπέλεκκον ‘half-axe’ are the two prizes; what made the second ‘half’ of the first is not known, and a single blade is the usual guess.

sentences.t:
ἱστὸν δ’ ἔστησεν νηὸς κυανοπρῴροιο
τηλοῦ ἐπὶ ψαμάθοις,
sentences.l:
and a mast he set up of a dark-prowed ship
far off on the sands,
sentences.i: and he set up the mast of a dark-prowed ship far off on the sands,
sentences.n: ἱστόν is here a ship’s ‘mast’, the post that holds the target; the same word also means ‘loom’. ἔστησεν is the aorist of ἵστημι ‘set up’, and νηὸς κυανοπρῴροιο ‘of a dark-prowed ship’ is the stock phrase for a ship. ψαμάθοις is the epic dative plural of ψάμαθος ‘sand’, and τηλοῦ ‘far off’ puts the mast far from the archers.

sentences.t:
ἐκ δὲ τρήρωνα πέλειαν
λεπτῇ μηρίνθῳ δῆσεν ποδός,
sentences.l:
and from it a timorous dove
with a thin cord he bound by the foot,
sentences.i: and he tied a timorous dove by the foot with a thin cord to it,
sentences.n: ἐκ δέ … δῆσεν is tmesis, ‘tied from’, with the mast of the line before understood as what the cord hangs from. τρήρων is an adjective ‘timorous’ beside πέλεια ‘dove’ (the same word as the Odyssey’s τρήρωνες at 12.63). μήρινθος is ‘cord’, here λεπτῇ ‘thin’, and ποδός is the genitive ‘by the foot’. The unit begins in the middle of line 853.

sentences.t:
ἧς ἄρ’ ἀνώγει
τοξεύειν·
sentences.l:
at which then he bade them
shoot:
sentences.i: he bade them shoot at it:
sentences.n: ἧς is the genitive of the relative, ‘at which’, because τοξεύειν ‘to shoot’ takes a genitive. ἀνώγει ‘bade’ is a past tense of ἄνωγα, and its object ‘them’, the archers, is understood. The colon introduces Achilles’ rule for the prize, which runs to the end of line 858. The unit begins in the middle of line 854.

sentences.t:
ὃς μέν κε βάλῃ τρήρωνα πέλειαν,
πάντας ἀειράμενος πελέκεας οἶκον δὲ φερέσθω·
sentences.l:
“whoever shall hit the timorous dove,
having taken up all the axes, let him carry them homeward;
sentences.i: “Whoever hits the timorous dove, let him take up all the axes and carry them home;
sentences.n: ὃς … κε βάλῃ ‘whoever shall hit’ is the general subjunctive with κε. ἀειράμενος is the aorist participle of ἀείρω ‘lift’, and φερέσθω a middle imperative, ‘let him carry off for himself’; οἶκον δέ is ‘homeward’. The rule is given in Achilles’ own words, as commands that follow ἀνώγει ‘bade’ in the line before (φερέσθω is a third-person imperative, which narration would not use), so it is set in quotation marks. The unit begins in the middle of line 855.
sentences.mark: Achilles states the rule for the archers

sentences.t:
ὃς δέ κε μηρίνθοιο τύχῃ ὄρνιθος ἁμαρτών,
ἥσσων γὰρ δὴ κεῖνος, ὃ δ’ οἴσεται ἡμιπέλεκκα.
sentences.l:
and whoever shall hit the cord, missing the bird,
for lesser is that man indeed, he shall carry off the half-axes.”
sentences.i: and whoever hits the cord and misses the bird, being the lesser, shall carry off the half-axes.”
sentences.n: τύχῃ ‘hit’ takes the genitive μηρίνθοιο ‘cord’, and ἁμαρτών is the aorist participle ‘having missed’, with ὄρνιθος ‘the bird’, the dove. ἥσσων ‘lesser’ is the archer who only cuts the cord, and γάρ gives the reason for his smaller prize. οἴσεται ‘he shall carry off’ is the future of φέρω. The closing quotation mark ends the rule.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἔφατ’, ὦρτο δ’ ἔπειτα βίη Τεύκροιο ἄνακτος,
ἂν δ’ ἄρα Μηριόνης θεράπων ἐῢς Ἰδομενῆος.
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and rose then the might of lord Teucer,
and up rose Meriones, good attendant of Idomeneus.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and the might of lord Teucer rose, and up rose Meriones, the good attendant of Idomeneus.
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφατ’ and ὦρτο … ἂν δ’ ἄρα return, with the same tmesis as at 811. βίη Τεύκροιο ἄνακτος ‘the might of lord Teucer’ is a periphrasis for Teucer, like Πριάμοιο βίην for Priam at 3.105. Μηριόνης θεράπων ἐῢς Ἰδομενῆος is ‘Meriones, good attendant of Idomeneus’, the Cretan leader.

sentences.t: κλήρους δ’ ἐν κυνέῃ χαλκήρεϊ πάλλον ἑλόντες,
sentences.l: and lots in a bronze-fitted helmet they shook, having taken them,
sentences.i: and they took lots and shook them in a bronze-fitted helmet,
sentences.n: κλήροι ‘lots’ are marks or tokens that are shaken together, and the pair take them (ἑλόντες ‘having taken’) and shake them (πάλλον) in a helmet; the same line stands at 3.316, where Hector and Odysseus draw lots. κυνέῃ χαλκήρεϊ ‘bronze-fitted helmet’ is a stock phrase. The subject, the two archers, is understood from the line before.

sentences.t: Τεῦκρος δὲ πρῶτος κλήρῳ λάχεν·
sentences.l: and Teucer first by lot obtained;
sentences.i: and Teucer drew the first turn by lot;
sentences.n: λάχεν is the aorist of λαγχάνω ‘obtain by lot’, and κλήρῳ ‘by lot’ is a dative of means. The Greek gives it no object; πρῶτος ‘first’ implies that he drew the first turn, which the next unit confirms. The unit stops in the middle of line 862.

sentences.t:
αὐτίκα δ’ ἰὸν
ἧκεν ἐπικρατέως, οὐδ’ ἠπείλησεν ἄνακτι
ἀρνῶν πρωτογόνων ῥέξειν κλειτὴν ἑκατόμβην.
sentences.l:
and at once an arrow
he let go mightily, and did not promise the lord
of first-born lambs to sacrifice a famous hecatomb.
sentences.i: and at once he let the arrow fly mightily, but he did not promise the lord to sacrifice a famous hecatomb of first-born lambs.
sentences.n: ἰόν is ‘arrow’ (ἰός), and ἧκεν ‘let go’; ἐπικρατέως ‘mightily’ describes the shot. ἠπείλησεν is the aorist of ἀπειλέω ‘threaten’, but with a god in the dative and a future infinitive of sacrifice it means ‘promise, vow’; the same use recurs at 872. ἄνακτι ‘the lord’ is Apollo, named in the next line. ῥέξειν ‘to sacrifice’ takes κλειτὴν ἑκατόμβην ‘a famous hecatomb’ and ἀρνῶν πρωτογόνων ‘of first-born lambs’.

sentences.t: ὄρνιθος μὲν ἅμαρτε· μέγηρε γάρ οἱ τό γ’ Ἀπόλλων·
sentences.l: the bird indeed he missed; for grudged him that Apollo;
sentences.i: He missed the bird, for Apollo grudged him that;
sentences.n: ἅμαρτε is the aorist of ἁμαρτάνω ‘miss’, with the genitive ὄρνιθος ‘the bird’, the dove. μέγηρε ‘grudged’ is the aorist of μεγαίρω, with οἱ ‘him’ in the dative and τό γ’ ‘that at least’ in the accusative. The poet explains the miss by the god’s grudge, and the reason is the vow Teucer left out in the last unit.

sentences.t: αὐτὰρ ὃ μήρινθον βάλε πὰρ πόδα, τῇ δέδετ’ ὄρνις·
sentences.l: but he hit the cord beside the foot, where the bird was tied;
sentences.i: but he struck the cord beside the foot, where the bird was tied;
sentences.n: βάλε ‘hit’ has μήρινθον ‘cord’ as its object, and πὰρ πόδα (πὰρ is παρά elided) puts the hit ‘beside the foot’, where the bird was tied. δέδετ’ is an elided perfect passive of δέω ‘bind’, either δέδεται ‘is tied’ or δέδετο ‘was tied’; the English takes the past. The cord is hit, not the bird.

sentences.t: ἀντικρὺ δ’ ἀπὸ μήρινθον τάμε πικρὸς ὀϊστός.
sentences.l: and right through, the cord cut the bitter arrow.
sentences.i: and the bitter arrow cut the cord clean through.
sentences.n: ἀπὸ … τάμε is tmesis, ‘cut off’ (τάμε is ἔταμε, aorist of τέμνω without the augment), and ἀντικρύ ‘straight through’ says the cut was clean. πικρὸς ὀϊστός ‘the bitter arrow’ is a stock phrase. Teucer’s shot frees the dove.

sentences.t:
ἣ μὲν ἔπειτ’ ἤϊξε πρὸς οὐρανόν, ἣ δὲ παρείθη
μήρινθος ποτὶ γαῖαν·
sentences.l:
She indeed then darted to the sky, but the cord
hung loose toward the earth;
sentences.i: The bird darted up toward the sky, and the cord hung loose toward the earth;
sentences.n: ἣ μέν … ἣ δέ ‘the one … the other’ sets the bird against the cord (ἣ is the article as a pronoun). ἤϊξε is the aorist of ἀΐσσω ‘dart’, and παρείθη the aorist passive of παρίημι ‘let go, slacken’, so the cord ‘was let slip, hung loose’. ποτί is πρός ‘toward’. The unit ends in the middle of line 869.

sentences.t: ἀτὰρ κελάδησαν Ἀχαιοί.
sentences.l: but they shouted aloud, the Achaeans.
sentences.i: and the Achaeans shouted aloud.
sentences.n: ἀτάρ ‘but’ turns from the cord to the crowd. κελάδησαν ‘shouted aloud’ is the aorist of κελαδέω; the Greek says nothing of the mood of the shout, whether it is for the shot or for the near miss. The unit begins in the middle of line 869.

sentences.t:
σπερχόμενος δ’ ἄρα Μηριόνης ἐξείρυσε χειρὸς
τόξον·
sentences.l:
And Meriones, hurrying, pulled out from his hand
the bow;
sentences.i: And Meriones, in haste, pulled the bow out of Teucer’s hand;
sentences.n: σπερχόμενος ‘hurrying’ is the participle of σπέρχομαι. ἐξείρυσε is the aorist of ἐξερύω ‘pull out’, with χειρός, the genitive of separation, ‘out of the hand’: the hand is Teucer’s, since Meriones draws the second turn. The unit ends in the middle of line 871.

sentences.t: ἀτὰρ δὴ ὀϊστὸν ἔχεν πάλαι, ὡς ἴθυνεν.
sentences.l: but he had an arrow in hand for some time, while he guided it straight.
sentences.i: but he had been holding an arrow for some time, while Teucer took aim.
sentences.n: ἀτὰρ δή ‘but indeed’ adds that Meriones was ready: ἔχεν is an unaugmented imperfect of ἔχω, and πάλαι ‘for some time’ means he had held the arrow while Teucer shot. The subject of ὡς ἴθυνεν ‘while he aimed’ (ἰθύνω ‘guide straight’) is not named; the natural reading is Teucer, taking aim, as the English says. The unit begins in the middle of line 871.

sentences.t:
αὐτίκα δ’ ἠπείλησεν ἑκηβόλῳ Ἀπόλλωνι
ἀρνῶν πρωτογόνων ῥέξειν κλειτὴν ἑκατόμβην.
sentences.l:
and at once he promised far-shooting Apollo
of first-born lambs to sacrifice a famous hecatomb.
sentences.i: At once he promised far-shooting Apollo to sacrifice a famous hecatomb of first-born lambs.
sentences.n: ἠπείλησεν ‘promised’ is the verb of 863, with ἑκηβόλῳ Ἀπόλλωνι ‘far-shooting Apollo’ in the dative. Lines 872b–873 repeat Teucer’s omitted vow (863–864) almost word for word: Meriones makes the vow Teucer left out. ῥέξειν takes κλειτὴν ἑκατόμβην and ἀρνῶν πρωτογόνων, as before.

sentences.t: ὕψι δ’ ὑπὸ νεφέων εἶδε τρήρωνα πέλειαν·
sentences.l: and high under the clouds he saw the timorous dove;
sentences.i: and high up beneath the clouds he saw the timorous dove;
sentences.n: ὕψι ‘high’ and ὑπὸ νεφέων ‘under the clouds’ (the genitive after ὑπό) place the dove where it has flown since the cord was cut. εἶδε is the aorist of ὁράω ‘saw’; the subject, Meriones, is understood. τρήρωνα πέλειαν is the same phrase as at 853.

sentences.t: τῇ ῥ’ ὅ γε δινεύουσαν ὑπὸ πτέρυγος βάλε μέσσην,
sentences.l: there as she circled he struck her under the wing, in the middle,
sentences.i: and as she wheeled there he hit her in the middle, under the wing,
sentences.n: τῇ ‘there’ and ῥ’ (ῥα) are particles, and ὅ γε ‘he’ is Meriones. δινεύουσαν ‘wheeling’ is a participle agreeing with the dove, the object; ὑπὸ πτέρυγος ‘under the wing’ says where, and μέσσην ‘in the middle’ also agrees with the dove. βάλε is the aorist of βάλλω ‘hit’.

sentences.t: ἀντικρὺ δὲ διῆλθε βέλος·
sentences.l: and right through went the shaft;
sentences.i: and the shaft went right through;
sentences.n: ἀντικρύ ‘straight through’ and διῆλθε ‘passed through’, the aorist of διέρχομαι, say that the arrow went clean through the dove. βέλος ‘shaft’ is the house word for the missile; ὀϊστός is the word for ‘arrow’ in the stock phrase of 867.

sentences.t:
τὸ μὲν ἂψ ἐπὶ γαίῃ
πρόσθεν Μηριόναο πάγη ποδός·
sentences.l:
and it back on the earth
before the foot of Meriones stuck;
sentences.i: and it came back down and stuck in the earth in front of Meriones’ foot;
sentences.n: τὸ μέν ‘it’ is the shaft, which comes ἂψ ‘back’ down to the ground. πάγη is the aorist passive of πήγνυμι ‘fix, stick’, and ποδός is the genitive after πρόσθεν ‘in front of’. Μηριόναο is the epic genitive in -αο, possessive with ποδός. Line 877 is metrically irregular as transmitted: Μηριόναο fits the verse only if the syllable να is read long. The sentence is set against the bird in the next unit by μέν … αὐτάρ.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἣ ὄρνις
ἱστῷ ἐφεζομένη νηὸς κυανοπρῴροιο
αὐχέν’ ἀπεκρέμασεν, σὺν δὲ πτερὰ πυκνὰ λίασθεν.
sentences.l:
but the bird
settling on the mast of the dark-prowed ship
hung down her neck, and her close-set wings sank together.
sentences.i: but the bird, settling on the mast of the dark-prowed ship, let her neck hang down, and her close-set wings sank together.
sentences.n: ἣ ὄρνις ‘the bird’ has the article as a demonstrative. ἐφεζομένη ‘settling on’ takes the dative ἱστῷ ‘mast’, the one she had been tied to. ἀπεκρέμασεν is the aorist of ἀποκρεμάννυμι ‘let hang down’, with αὐχέν’ ‘neck’ as its object. σὺν … λίασθεν is tmesis: the wings sank ‘together’ (λίασθεν, aorist passive of λιάζομαι ‘sink, give way’); πτερὰ πυκνά are the close-set wings. The unit begins in the middle of line 877, where ἣ before ὄρνις is shortened in the verse (correption), the second irregularity of the line.

sentences.t:
ὠκὺς δ’ ἐκ μελέων θυμὸς πτάτο, τῆλε δ’ ἀπ’ αὐτοῦ
κάππεσε·
sentences.l:
and swift from her limbs the spirit flew, and far from it
she fell;
sentences.i: and the swift spirit flew from her limbs, and she fell far from the mast;
sentences.n: ὠκὺς … θυμός ‘the swift spirit’ leaves the limbs (μελέων, the genitive after ἐκ); πτάτο is the aorist of πέτομαι ‘flew’, without the augment. κάππεσε is κατέπεσε ‘fell down’, and ἀπ’ αὐτοῦ ‘from it’ most naturally refers to the mast (ἱστός, a masculine noun; the bird herself would be αὐτῆς), so the dead bird falls far from it. The unit ends in the middle of line 881.

sentences.t: λαοὶ δ’ αὖ θηεῦντό τε θάμβησάν τε.
sentences.l: and the people in turn both gazed and were struck with wonder.
sentences.i: and the people gazed, and were struck with wonder.
sentences.n: λαοί is ‘the people’, the onlookers, and αὖ ‘in turn’ marks the change of subject. θηεῦντο ‘gazed’ is the imperfect of θηέομαι, and θάμβησαν ‘were struck with wonder’ the aorist of θαμβέω (θάμβος ‘wonder’ is its noun). τε … τε ties the two verbs together, ‘both … and’. The same line stands at 728, where the onlookers watch the wrestling. The unit begins in the middle of line 881.

sentences.t:
ἂν δ’ ἄρα Μηριόνης πελέκεας δέκα πάντας ἄειρε,
Τεῦκρος δ’ ἡμιπέλεκκα φέρεν κοίλας ἐπὶ νῆας.
sentences.l:
and up Meriones all ten axes lifted,
and Teucer the half-axes bore to the hollow ships.
sentences.i: And Meriones took up all ten axes, and Teucer carried the half-axes to the hollow ships.
sentences.n: ἂν … ἄειρε is tmesis, ‘lifted up’; ἄειρε is a past tense of ἀείρω. The ten axes (πελέκεας δέκα) are all the πελέκεας of 851, Meriones’ prize for the hit, and Teucer takes the ἡμιπέλεκκα, the lesser prize for cutting the cord. φέρεν is the unaugmented imperfect of φέρω, ‘was carrying’. κοίλας ἐπὶ νῆας is ‘to the hollow ships’.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ Πηλεΐδης κατὰ μὲν δολιχόσκιον ἔγχος,
κὰδ δὲ λέβητ’ ἄπυρον βοὸς ἄξιον ἀνθεμόεντα
θῆκ’ ἐς ἀγῶνα φέρων·
sentences.i: Then the son of Peleus brought the long-shadowed spear and an unfired cauldron worth an ox, decorated with flowers, and set them down in the gathering;
sentences.n: A third contest begins, the javelin-throw. κατὰ μέν … κὰδ δέ … θῆκ’ … φέρων is tmesis again, with two objects, the long-shadowed spear and the cauldron (λέβης). ἄπυρον ‘unfired’ means not yet put on a fire, so new; βοὸς ἄξιον ‘worth an ox’ gives its value; ἀνθεμόεντα, from ἄνθεμον ‘flower’, means ‘flowery’, here presumably a pattern of flowers on the metal.

sentences.t: καί ῥ’ ἥμονες ἄνδρες ἀνέσταν·
sentences.l: and throwing men stood up;
sentences.i: and men who throw stood up;
sentences.n: ἥμονες is formed from ἵημι ‘send, throw’ and is taken as ‘throwers’, as the contest is a throw of the spear; the Greek names no weapon. ἀνέσταν is ἀνέστησαν, ‘stood up’, and ῥ’ is ῥα. The unit begins in the middle of line 886.

sentences.t:
ἂν μὲν ἄρ’ Ἀτρεΐδης εὐρὺ κρείων Ἀγαμέμνων,
ἂν δ’ ἄρα Μηριόνης, θεράπων ἐῢς Ἰδομενῆος.
sentences.l:
up indeed rose Atreus’-son, wide-ruling Agamemnon,
and up Meriones, good attendant of Idomeneus.
sentences.i: Up stood Agamemnon, son of Atreus, wide-ruling, and up stood Meriones, the good attendant of Idomeneus.
sentences.n: ἂν μέν … ἂν δ’ … has no verb of its own; ἀνέσταν of the line before supplies it, ‘up (they stood)’. Ἀτρεΐδης is Agamemnon, and εὐρὺ κρείων ‘wide-ruling’ is his stock title (printed as two words). Μηριόνης θεράπων ἐῢς Ἰδομενῆος is the same phrase as at 860.

sentences.t: τοῖσι δὲ καὶ μετέειπε ποδάρκης δῖος Ἀχιλλεύς·
sentences.l: and among them also spoke swift-footed, heavenly Achilles:
sentences.i: Swift-footed, heavenly Achilles also spoke among them:
sentences.n: τοῖσι ‘to them’ means the throwers standing up, and μετέειπε is ‘spoke among’ (aorist of μετεῖπον). καί ‘also’ adds this speech to those he has already made at the games. ποδάρκης δῖος Ἀχιλλεύς ‘swift-footed, heavenly Achilles’ is his stock title. The colon introduces his speech to Agamemnon, which runs to line 894.

sentences.t:
Ἀτρεΐδη· ἴδμεν γὰρ ὅσον προβέβηκας ἁπάντων
ἠδ’ ὅσσον δυνάμει τε καὶ ἥμασιν ἔπλευ ἄριστος·
sentences.l:
“Atreus’-son, for we know how far you surpass all
and how much in power and in throws you have become the best;
sentences.i: “Son of Atreus, for we know how far you surpass all, and how much you have become the best in power and in throws;
sentences.n: Ἀτρεΐδη is the vocative ‘son of Atreus’, Agamemnon. ἴδμεν is ἴσμεν ‘we know’, and the clause ὅσον … ἠδ’ ὅσσον ‘how far … and how much’ is an indirect question. προβέβηκας (perfect of προβαίνω, ‘you have gone ahead’) takes the genitive ἁπάντων ‘of all’. ἥμασιν is the dative plural of ἧμα ‘throw’, from ἵημι, and ἔπλευ is the contracted ἔπλεο from πέλομαι, ‘you have become’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ σὺ μὲν τόδ’ ἄεθλον ἔχων κοίλας ἐπὶ νῆας
ἔρχευ, ἀτὰρ δόρυ Μηριόνῃ ἥρωϊ πόρωμεν,
sentences.l:
but you, this contest-prize taking, to the hollow ships
go, and the spear to Meriones the hero let us give,
sentences.i: but you take this prize and go to the hollow ships, and let us give the spear to Meriones the hero,
sentences.n: ἔχων ‘having’ goes with ἔρχευ, the imperative of ἔρχομαι, ‘go’, so ‘go with this prize’: the cauldron of 885. πόρωμεν is the aorist subjunctive of πορεῖν ‘give’, in a hortatory sense, ‘let us give’, with δόρυ ‘spear’ (the spear of 884) as object and Μηριόνῃ ἥρωϊ ‘to Meriones the hero’ in the dative. ἄεθλον is ‘prize’.

sentences.t: εἰ σύ γε σῷ θυμῷ ἐθέλοις· κέλομαι γὰρ ἔγωγε.
sentences.l: if you in your heart are willing; for I at least urge it.”
sentences.i: if you are willing in your heart; I for my part urge it.”
sentences.n: εἰ … ἐθέλοις is an optative clause, ‘if you should be willing’, which softens the proposal. κέλομαι ‘I urge’ gives the speaker’s reason, γάρ, and ἔγωγε ‘I at least’ stresses that it is his own wish. θυμῷ is ‘heart’. The closing quotation mark ends Achilles’ speech, which began at 890.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἔφατ’, οὐδ’ ἀπίθησεν ἄναξ ἀνδρῶν Ἀγαμέμνων·
δῶκε δὲ Μηριόνῃ δόρυ χάλκεον·
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and did not disobey, the lord of men, Agamemnon;
and he gave to Meriones the bronze spear;
sentences.i: So Achilles spoke, and Agamemnon, lord of men, did not disobey; and he gave Meriones the bronze spear;
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφατ’ ‘So he spoke’; οὐδ’ ἀπίθησεν ‘and did not disobey’ (aorist of ἀπιθέω) is the formula for assent, here Agamemnon’s, whom the Greek names ἄναξ ἀνδρῶν ‘lord of men’. The throw is thus never held: Achilles gives the prize without a contest and Agamemnon agrees. δόρυ χάλκεον ‘the bronze spear’ is the spear of 884. The unit ends in the middle of line 896.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ὅ γ’ ἥρως
Ταλθυβίῳ κήρυκι δίδου περικαλλὲς ἄεθλον.
sentences.l:
but he, the hero,
to Talthybius the herald gave the very fair contest-prize.
sentences.i: But the hero himself handed the very fair prize to Talthybius the herald.
sentences.n: αὐτὰρ ὅ γ’ ἥρως ‘but he, the hero’, is Agamemnon, who hands the cauldron (περικαλλὲς ἄεθλον ‘very fair prize’, 885) to Talthybius, his herald. δίδου is the imperfect of δίδωμι without the augment, and κήρυκι ‘herald’ is dative. The part ends with the prizes disposed of. The unit begins in the middle of line 896.
